evidence_check.title: An AI support app can comfort and hold attention
evidence_check.finding: HBS reports both short-term well-being gains from a prevention-focused AI coach in a randomized study of nearly 500 US students and attachment, harmful-interaction and crisis-response concerns in AI companion studies.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a personal reply can feel supportive while also making it harder to leave, question or move toward human care.
evidence_check.counterpoint: An app can provide private, low-cost support when human care is hard to reach. A short-term well-being gain is real even though it is not the same as diagnosis or treatment.
evidence_check.limit: The current studies do not show long-term US outcomes, the share of users harmed or a safe route to human care for every product.
evidence_check.location: HBS Working Knowledge reports on AI emotional support and companion apps, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: An AI support app can comfort and hold attention
nodes.summary: AI emotional support can bring short-term relief while creating attachment, safety and exit questions.
nodes.question: When does private support become a private care gap?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not show long-term safety or the full route to human care.

evidence_check.title: Older consumers are not one market
evidence_check.finding: HBS reports that older customers differ in health and activity while often holding substantial buying power, repeat buying and influence on younger consumers. NBER evidence shows that spending and satisfaction at older ages also vary with health, widowhood and changing enjoyment.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: age alone hides different needs, resources and risks, so the same product or service can help one older customer and miss another.
evidence_check.counterpoint: More detailed targeting can improve fit, but it can also lead to exclusion, higher prices or pressure to buy. Lower spending may be a choice, loss or constraint.
evidence_check.limit: The current sources do not show whether better marketing or age-friendly design improves older people's financial, health or service outcomes.
evidence_check.location: HBS Working Knowledge, May 7, 2026; NBER aging studies checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Older consumers are not one market
nodes.summary: Health, wealth, independence and living situation can matter more than age alone.
nodes.question: Who benefits from being seen as an older customer?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not connect targeting to better household or service outcomes.

evidence_check.title: Households may hear a rate increase as a price warning
evidence_check.finding: An NBER survey of more than 25,000 US households with randomized information treatments finds that people expect higher rates to raise borrowing costs and inflation, report reducing spending especially on durable goods, and change portfolios in response to inflation expectations.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: monetary policy may reach households through their beliefs about future prices, not only through the loan rate they directly face.
evidence_check.counterpoint: A borrower, saver and renter can face opposite effects. Reported beliefs are not the same as actual spending, debt or portfolio records.
evidence_check.limit: The current evidence does not show which households receive the message, change behavior and bear the cost in their financial records.
evidence_check.location: Grigoli, Sandri, Gorodnichenko and Coibion, Monetary Policy According to Households, NBER Working Paper 35127, April 2026. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Households may hear a rate increase as a price warning
nodes.summary: Household beliefs about rates, prices and borrowing can shape spending and saving in different ways.
nodes.question: How does a rate decision become a household choice?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not match beliefs to actual household financial records.

evidence_check.title: The hometown tie in entrepreneurship has weakened
evidence_check.finding: HBS reports that US-born self-employed White men were only 2 percentage points more likely than wage workers to stay in their birth state in 2018, down from an 8-point difference in 1970; the local advantage fell below zero for all Americans in the latest sample.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: local business ownership may be less tied to local networks and more tied to mobile capital, skills and opportunity.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Moving can help founders find customers, workers and capital. Birthplace is not the same as commitment, and local ownership is not always better for residents.
evidence_check.limit: The current evidence measures where self-employed people stay, not local business survival, services, jobs, prices or belonging.
evidence_check.location: HBS Working Knowledge, reporting Colaiacovo, Dalton, Sari Pekkala Kerr and William Kerr, August 28, 2026. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: The hometown tie in entrepreneurship has weakened
nodes.summary: Would-be business owners are less likely to stay near where they were born.
nodes.question: What does a place lose when ownership moves?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not measure local services, jobs or customer outcomes.

evidence_check.title: The vote may respond more to lost buying power than inflation alone
evidence_check.finding: A new NBER county study of the United States from 2021–2024 reports that real-wage decline, rather than higher inflation alone, predicts Republican electoral gains, while inflation remains associated with presidential vote share beyond that measure.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the political meaning of prices may depend on whether local pay keeps up with local costs.
evidence_check.counterpoint: County results do not show how each person voted, and party identity, social issues, media and local candidates can outweigh economic conditions.
evidence_check.limit: The current evidence does not join one household's prices, wages, blame, trust and vote choice.
evidence_check.location: Riaño and Trebbi, Do Voters Punish Inflation or Pay Cuts? Inflation and Real Wages in US Elections, NBER Working Paper 35301, June 2026. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: The vote may respond more to lost buying power than inflation alone
nodes.summary: Local pay falling behind local costs may matter more than the national inflation rate by itself.
nodes.question: What economic loss reaches the ballot?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence is county-level and does not identify each voter's reason.

evidence_check.title: Privacy rules can make people more willing to share
evidence_check.finding: HBS reports that users of one receipt-and-reward app in California and Virginia shared 9% more information after privacy rules took effect, including more receipts, store visits and retail categories. The research points to trust as a key mechanism.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a privacy rule can change the feeling of the exchange, not only the legal terms, and may increase both customer comfort and firm knowledge.
evidence_check.counterpoint: More sharing may be useful when the deal is clear, but it can also give a firm more power to predict, target or price a person. Consent is not the same as equal bargaining power.
evidence_check.limit: The current evidence comes from one platform and does not show that users understood later data uses or received better outcomes.
evidence_check.location: HBS Working Knowledge, reporting Demirci, Israeli and Ascarza, In Privacy We Trust, Working Paper 26-001, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Privacy rules can make people more willing to share
nodes.summary: Clearer privacy control may increase data sharing while also increasing what firms know about customers.
nodes.question: Who gains when trust opens the door to more data?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not measure later data use, customer outcomes or equal bargaining power.

evidence_check.title: Staying with one bank can carry a quiet cost
evidence_check.finding: NBER reports that only 5–15% of depositors open a new account each year and estimates that depositor inactivity accounts for 57% of average deposit franchise value. The study also finds that inactivity reduced modeled default probabilities during the 2023 banking turmoil.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the same habit that may cost a customer interest can give a bank cheaper, steadier funding.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Staying can be rational when bill tools, local access, trust, safety or switching time matter. More switching may also make bank funding less stable.
evidence_check.limit: The current evidence does not show the interest lost by each household or the net value of switching after fees, convenience and bank risk.
evidence_check.location: Egan, Hortaçsu, Kaplan, Sunderam and Yao, Dynamic Competition for Sleepy Deposits, NBER Working Paper 34267, revised March 2026. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Staying with one bank can carry a quiet cost
nodes.summary: Bank habits can leave value with the bank while also helping keep funding steady.
nodes.question: What is convenience worth in lost interest?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not measure each household's net cost or benefit.

evidence_check.title: Equal income can buy a different life through several jobs
evidence_check.finding: HBS reports that similarly paid people working multiple jobs spent less of take-home pay, less on necessities and less on extras, while carrying higher transportation costs and saving less.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the number and structure of jobs can shape household life even when income looks similar.
evidence_check.counterpoint: People may choose multiple jobs for flexibility, school, care or a job transition. Lower spending may reflect a deliberate goal or a different need, not only strain caused by the work arrangement.
evidence_check.limit: The current evidence does not identify whether instability, worker choice, family need, education, health or multiple jobs itself drives the spending pattern.
evidence_check.location: HBS Working Knowledge, reporting Tsai and Buell, The Hidden Costs of Working Multiple Jobs, Working Paper 25-036, revised March 2025. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Equal income can buy a different life through several jobs
nodes.summary: Multiple jobs can change spending, travel and saving even when take-home pay is similar.
nodes.question: What does equal income fail to show?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not isolate the cause or measure the full value of flexibility.

evidence_check.title: A monthly charge can survive after its value fades
evidence_check.finding: The NBER payment-card study finds a sharp rise in cancellations when replaced cards force subscribers to actively renew. The authors estimate that inattention raises seller revenue by 14% to more than 200% compared with a model where customers cancel as soon as value falls below price.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: automatic renewal can turn lost attention into recurring revenue, while the customer's cost stays hard to see until a forced choice.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Automatic renewal also prevents useful services from stopping, and the study does not prove that every customer who failed to cancel had stopped valuing the product.
evidence_check.limit: The sample covers one card network and 2017–2021; the model range is not a direct loss for every customer or a current estimate of total US household burden.
evidence_check.location: Einav, Klopack and Mahoney, Selling Subscriptions, NBER Working Paper 31547, August 2023. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A monthly charge can survive after its value fades
nodes.summary: Automatic renewal can turn a forgotten service into a recurring household cost.
nodes.question: When does convenience become inattention?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not yet measure current US household loss or cancellation effort.

evidence_check.title: A trade policy can reach the shelf slowly
evidence_check.finding: NBER estimates about 20% retail pass-through from the 2025 US tariffs in the short run, while HBS reports that consumers carried an estimated 43% of the tariff burden after seven months and firms carried the rest.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a tariff can be politically visible when announced but economically quiet at first, with the household effect arriving later through prices, product choice or margins.
evidence_check.counterpoint: The price path can also reflect sourcing, retailer decisions, demand and other costs. Tariffs may change jobs or production in ways a shelf-price study does not measure.
evidence_check.limit: The current studies do not show the exact bill, purchase change or political response for the same US household.
evidence_check.location: Cavallo, Llamas and Vazquez, Tracking the Short-Run Price Impact of US Tariffs, NBER Working Paper 34496, November 2025; HBS update checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A trade policy can reach the shelf slowly
nodes.summary: Tariffs can move from policy to importer cost to shelf price through a delayed and partial path.
nodes.question: Who pays, and when does the cost become visible?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not join policy, household purchases, wages and political response.

evidence_check.title: A slower rise in prices can still feel like a loss
evidence_check.finding: NBER surveys of representative US samples report that people mainly dislike inflation because they believe buying power falls when wages do not keep up with prices. HBS retail-price analysis also reports faster increases for the cheapest food products than for the most expensive during the recent inflation period.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: people may read inflation through repeated low-cost purchases and wage comparisons, not only through the national rate.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Survey beliefs are not the same as measured household loss, and a few visible prices may stand in for a much wider basket shaped by income, housing, debt and place.
evidence_check.limit: The current sources do not follow the same household from price and wage changes to purchases, trust or voting.
evidence_check.location: Stantcheva, Why Do We Dislike Inflation?, NBER Working Paper 32300, 2024; HBS price analysis checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A slower rise in prices can still feel like a loss
nodes.summary: People may judge inflation through the cheap goods and wages they see repeatedly.
nodes.question: Which price becomes the story of the economy?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not join actual household prices, wages and political response.

evidence_check.title: The same checkout price can hide different payment costs
evidence_check.finding: Using merchant payment data, researchers estimate that interchange fees move about $30 billion a year from cash and debit users to credit-card users. Different shoppers and different merchant fees reduce the estimated transfer by about 25%, but do not remove it.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the visible price does not tell us who funds the rewards. Payment choice, income and where people shop can change the result for a household.
evidence_check.limit: The estimate depends on how fee costs pass through to prices and on the study's merchant and survey data. It is not a bill charged directly to each debit or cash user, and it does not prove hardship for every lower-income household.
evidence_check.location: Egan, Matvos, Seru, Wang and Yao, Who Pays for Payments?, NBER Working Paper 35067, April 2026 abstract. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: The price on the screen is only part of the cost
nodes.summary: Fees, rewards and payment timing can leave households with different costs for the same purchase.
nodes.question: Who pays beyond the purchase price?
nodes.limit: The current payment finding relies on an HBS summary; the underlying paper still needs review.

evidence_check.title: Insurance can affect both the bill and the home's value
evidence_check.finding: Using more than 74 million insurance premiums inferred from mortgage payments in 2014–2024, researchers estimate that rising premiums reduced home-price growth by over $40,000 in the most exposed ZIP codes.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a household may face a higher running cost while its main asset gains less value. Check both bills and wealth when comparing housing pressure with other household costs.
evidence_check.limit: This is an estimated reduction in price growth, not a $40,000 loss for every homeowner. Only the indexed NBER abstract was reviewed in this pass; full methods remain unchecked. Moves and local-business effects are unproven.
evidence_check.location: Keys and Mulder, working paper, revised November 2025. Abstract checked through search on 2026-09-11; direct page returned 403.

nodes.title: Keeping a home also means paying to protect it
nodes.summary: Insurance bills and gaps in coverage belong in the housing affordability story.
nodes.question: Who can afford protection?
nodes.limit: The packet does not establish that insurance changes caused families to move.

evidence_check.title: A payment bridge can become a late-payment gap
evidence_check.finding: In the Federal Reserve's 2024 household survey, 15% of adults used buy now, pay later. Twenty-four percent of users paid late, including 40% of users with family income under $25,000; 57% of late users said they were charged extra.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a product can make the first purchase possible while making the next payment a new pressure. Compare the user's income, the product's terms and the later result.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Provider data tell a less severe story for the product market: the CFPB reports a 1.83% loan charge-off rate in 2023 and a 4.1% loan-level late-fee rate in its measures. These rates use different units from the Fed survey and do not cancel the household result.
evidence_check.limit: The Fed figures are self-reported and do not show the later balance, interest, missed payment or household outcome. The CFPB provider data cover six large firms and use different denominators.
evidence_check.location: Federal Reserve, Economic Well-Being of US Households in 2024, banking and credit section. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Credit can be a bridge and a later bill
nodes.summary: When cash cannot cover a surprise, credit can preserve a purchase while moving the payment into the future.
nodes.question: What does borrowing protect, and what does it make harder later?
nodes.limit: The opening packet measures intended payment choices, not the full path from borrowing to repayment or loss of access.

evidence_check.title: Payment trouble is not the same as a large balance
evidence_check.finding: The Federal Reserve reports that 20% of borrowers were behind on a student loan payment or in collections in 2024. The rate was 30% among borrowers who completed some college, a technical degree or an associate degree. The New York Fed reports about $1.66 trillion in student debt and 10.3% of balances 90 days or more delinquent in 2026 Q1.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the useful unit is not debt alone. It is debt paired with income, education, payment rule and the life choice that comes next.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Debt can finance education with a high return, and income-based repayment can protect some borrowers when earnings are low. A balance or delinquency rate alone does not establish a bad life outcome.
evidence_check.limit: The Fed survey and New York Fed credit panel use different units and may be affected by reporting changes. They do not follow a current borrower from payment trouble to housing, work or family choice.
evidence_check.location: Federal Reserve 2024 household survey and New York Fed student-debt data. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A student loan can follow a person into adult choices
nodes.summary: Student debt is a long-running credit claim that can meet work, housing and family decisions after school.
nodes.question: What does repayment make harder, and for whom?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures balances and payment trouble, not the full life-choice effect.

evidence_check.title: Food is where a money problem can become a daily condition
evidence_check.finding: USDA estimates that 13.7% of US households, or 18.3 million, were food insecure at some point in 2024; 5.4% experienced very low food security. In the Federal Reserve's shorter 2024 survey, 7% of adults said their household sometimes or often did not have enough to eat in the prior month, including 19% below $25,000 income and 2% at $100,000 or more.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: food hardship makes household pressure visible as a daily choice, not only as a balance or price measure. Keep annual food insecurity and one-month food insufficiency separate.
evidence_check.counterpoint: The national USDA rate was not statistically different from 2023, so a high level of hardship is not the same as a newly worsening trend. Food access also depends on household size, disability, stores, school meals and public programs.
evidence_check.limit: USDA and Fed measures use different questions and time windows. Neither shows whether a household used credit, skipped care or reduced energy use before the food outcome.
evidence_check.location: USDA ERS Household Food Security in the United States in 2024 and Federal Reserve 2024 household survey comparison. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Food is where a money problem becomes a daily condition
nodes.summary: A household can keep a bill current by changing what it buys, how much it eats, or who it asks for help.
nodes.question: Which need gives way when the budget does not stretch?
nodes.limit: The opening packet measures food hardship, not the order of the household's tradeoffs.

evidence_check.title: Removing old debt may leave today's choices unchanged
evidence_check.finding: Two randomized experiments forgave medical debt in collections. Researchers detected no average improvement in surveyed health, care use or financial wellness. Credit access improved modestly where the debt would otherwise have been reported.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: ask whether help changes today's available money or access to care. An old balance disappearing may work differently.
evidence_check.limit: This tests specific debt relief, not all help with medical costs. It does not show that medical debt is harmless.
evidence_check.location: Abstract and Introduction; published in Quarterly Journal of Economics, May 2025. Reviewed 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: People can pay the bills by giving up care
nodes.summary: Skipped treatment can keep spending down while leaving a need unmet.
nodes.question: What did the household give up?
nodes.limit: Reported skipped care does not establish later health or job outcomes.

evidence_check.title: Work can change before care starts
evidence_check.finding: A published study links reported caregiving to earnings records. Women had lower employment and earnings after care began relative to a matched group. Men entered care after substantial work disruptions.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: families may arrange care around both a relative's needs and who has lost paid work. The order of events matters when deciding what help would restore income.
evidence_check.limit: The publisher abstract was reviewed; full methods and subgroup tables remain unchecked. Matching is not random assignment. This does not show that all caregivers follow these paths or that care later causes borrowing.
evidence_check.location: Maestas, Messel and Truskinovsky; Journal of Labor Economics 42(S1), 2024, abstract. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A family can pay for care with time
nodes.summary: Unpaid help uses hours that could otherwise go to work, rest or other family needs.
nodes.question: Whose time covers the need?
nodes.limit: Care hours are not automatically lost work hours; employment effects need separate evidence.

evidence_check.title: Family time can replace a large cash payment
evidence_check.finding: The Federal Reserve reports that 24% of parents living with children under 13 used paid childcare in the prior week in 2024, with a median weekly cost of $240. Forty-six percent used some unpaid care. Census estimates that households with care problems lost an average of 65.8 work days in 2024.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a family can pay for care with money, unpaid time or work time. These are different forms of support and should not be collapsed into one cost.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Paid care can make work possible, and unpaid care can be chosen and helpful. The survey measures arrangements and reported work loss, not what would happen if care prices or supply changed.
evidence_check.limit: The Fed and Census figures are descriptive and use different samples and questions. They do not establish that childcare caused a particular parent to leave work or cut another need.
evidence_check.location: Census CPS ASEC child-care working paper and Federal Reserve 2024 household survey. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Family time can replace a large cash payment
nodes.summary: Childcare can take money, unpaid family hours, or paid work time, and the mix differs by household resources.
nodes.question: Who pays for care, and in what form?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures care arrangements and reported work loss, not the full household tradeoff.

evidence_check.title: A lost benefit can leave a lasting mark on economic views
evidence_check.finding: A working paper estimates that each $1,000 lost when the expanded 2021 Child Tax Credit expired lowered consumer sentiment by 1.7 points. Effects lasted nearly two years and were largest among lower-income families with multiple children.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: connect views of the economy to changes in household support as well as prices. Ask what money stopped arriving, not only what became more expensive.
evidence_check.limit: The study compares households with different benefit losses; it is not a randomized experiment. Only the indexed NBER abstract was reviewed in this pass. Full methods remain unchecked, and the reported result does not establish a change in votes.
evidence_check.location: Bastian and Harvey, working paper, revised August 2026. Abstract checked through search on 2026-09-11; direct page returned 403.

nodes.title: Personal finances and national mood can move apart
nodes.summary: People judge the economy through both their circumstances and their expectations about the country.
nodes.question: What explains the gap between experience and belief?
nodes.limit: The surveys do not show that bills caused a vote; party identity can shape economic views.

evidence_check.title: The form of public help changes what families buy
evidence_check.finding: A new NBER study comparing pandemic-era food and cash aid finds larger short-run food-store spending responses for in-kind and recurring benefits than for one-time and cash benefits.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: policy does not only set the amount of help. It also shapes what the help can do in the household's week.
evidence_check.counterpoint: A larger food-store response may reflect useful protection, but it may also reflect a tighter label. Cash can help with rent, medicine, transport or debt that food aid cannot cover.
evidence_check.limit: The new study covers pandemic-era programs and short-run food-store spending. It does not show lasting security, well-being or political trust.
evidence_check.location: Bonomo, Ruffini and Schanzenbach, Is a Dollar a Dollar? How Transfer Design Shapes Household Spending, NBER Working Paper 35698, September 2026. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: The form of public help changes what families buy
nodes.summary: Cash, food aid, one-time payments and monthly payments can have different short-run effects even at the same value.
nodes.question: Does the design of help fit the need?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not yet measure lasting household security or political response.

evidence_check.title: Losing help does not necessarily mean finding work
evidence_check.finding: Two NBER studies using linked administrative data found that SNAP work requirements increased program exits but did not increase employment in the studied settings. A separate study found that closing a SNAP enrollment office reduced participation in nearby census tracts by 7–9% over two years.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the rule or route to help can change the household's food support before it changes the household's work. Measure program exit and employment as separate outcomes.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Work rules are intended to encourage employment, and some people leave a program because their circumstances improve. The current studies are causal in their settings but do not show that every rule has the same effect.
evidence_check.limit: The studies use defined policy settings and administrative measures. They do not yet show the same household's food, debt or health outcome after losing access.
evidence_check.location: Cook and East, revised 2025 working paper; related NBER work on work requirements and office access. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Help can exist but be hard to keep
nodes.summary: Rules, renewal work and office distance can decide whether support reaches a household, even when the need remains.
nodes.question: What makes help disappear before the need does?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence shows participation and employment changes, not the full food or household outcome.

evidence_check.title: A payment problem can become a recovery problem
evidence_check.finding: The Federal Reserve reports that 21% of adults experienced financial fraud or scams in 2024. Among adults with non-credit-card fraud, 63% lost money and 32% said at least some was not recovered; the estimated net loss was $63 billion.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: fraud can remove money and also force a household to spend time proving what happened and seeking a decision. Trust depends on the recovery path, not only on prevention.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Credit-card fraud losses are usually not paid directly by consumers, and the Fed estimate is self-reported. FTC complaint data also measure reports, not the full number of incidents.
evidence_check.limit: The sources do not follow the same consumer from fraud to recovery, account use or trust. Reported losses and complaint counts understate or reshape the full event.
evidence_check.location: Federal Reserve 2024 household survey, financial fraud section. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A payment problem can become a recovery problem
nodes.summary: A scam can cost money, time and confidence in the institution that holds or moves it.
nodes.question: Who carries the loss, and who can get an answer?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures exposure and reports, not the full recovery or trust path.

evidence_check.title: A business application is not the same as a new employer
evidence_check.finding: Using linked records for US business applications and employer firms, researchers separate starting an idea from putting it into operation. High-startup places have many applications; low-startup places more often have a low rate of applications becoming employer firms.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a town can look active in business counts while still adding few firms with paid workers. Read applications, employer starts and jobs as separate steps.
evidence_check.limit: The paper describes differences across places; this pass does not show what caused them or whether services, local ownership or belonging changed. An application also does not tell us whether a firm survived.
evidence_check.location: Dinlersoz, Dunne, Haltiwanger and Penciakova, The Local Origins of Business Formation, NBER Working Paper 34881, February 2026 abstract. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Business counts do not tell us who belongs to a place
nodes.summary: Applications, lasting jobs and locally rooted owners describe different parts of a town's economy.
nodes.question: What stays in the community?
nodes.limit: Birth-state location is not hometown attachment; civic effects remain questions.

evidence_check.title: Faster work does not mean a large jump in solved problems
evidence_check.finding: In a study of about 5,000 customer-support agents at a US software company, an AI helper raised issues solved per hour by 13.8%. The share of chats marked resolved rose by only 1.3 percentage points, while customer satisfaction did not change in a meaningful way.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: measure the answer customers got, not only the speed or number of chats handled. A firm can serve more contacts without making each difficult problem much easier to fix.
evidence_check.limit: The tool supported human agents and was rolled out within one company. The resolution measure and customer-satisfaction measure have limits, and this study does not test appeals, repeat complaints or whether a person could overturn a decision.
evidence_check.location: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, Generative AI at Work, NBER Working Paper 31161; NBER Digest summary and revised paper checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A quicker reply may still leave a problem open
nodes.summary: Response speed, a friendly tone and successful resolution need separate measures.
nodes.question: Can someone actually fix the problem?
nodes.limit: The service experiment is one setting; its results do not establish a general loss of appeal rights.

evidence_check.title: A useful aid can feel like an admission
evidence_check.finding: HBS reports research in which people trusted a person described as using willpower more than one using a blocking app, and later rated people using commitment tools as having less integrity. Participants were also less likely to choose a tool when others might find out.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a product can solve a practical problem and still lose adoption if using it carries a social cost.
evidence_check.counterpoint: The research summary does not show that willpower is always weaker, that every aid works, or that social judgment is the main reason people avoid one.
evidence_check.limit: We do not yet have a current US consumer record linking aid choice, social judgment and later behavior for the same people.
evidence_check.location: HBS Working Knowledge, reporting research by Julian Zlatev and Ariella Kristal, October 15, 2024. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A useful tool can feel like an admission
nodes.summary: People may choose private willpower over a visible aid when using help feels socially revealing.
nodes.question: What does the tool say about the person?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not yet measure the full behavior-change path.

evidence_check.title: A farewell can become a prompt to stay
evidence_check.finding: An analysis of chats across six companion platforms found that more than 37% of conversations in which users tried to leave contained at least one tactic that encouraged them to continue. Those tactics were followed by longer use and more messages in the study.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: time spent after a person tries to leave should not be counted as simple satisfaction. The design of the exit moment may shape the result.
evidence_check.limit: This is a research story about companion apps and a working paper analysis; it does not measure all digital products, lasting harm or the financial value of the extra use. The study does not establish a change in political trust.
evidence_check.location: HBS Working Knowledge, October 2025; article reports analysis of six platforms. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A useful app can still make leaving difficult
nodes.summary: The reason a person stays matters when longer conversations benefit the company.
nodes.question: Does staying reflect help or pressure?
nodes.limit: Companion-app studies do not represent all chatbot users or establish lasting harm.

evidence_check.title: AI use is spreading widely but remains uneven at work
evidence_check.finding: A nationally representative US worker survey finds that generative AI is used across many occupations and tasks, but in most of them fewer than half of workers use it. Workers doing similar work therefore may be using very different tools.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the first divide may be inside the same job, between workers who have access, training or permission and those who do not. Study the work rules around the tool, not only the tool itself.
evidence_check.counterpoint: In a separate randomized field experiment across 66 firms, workers who used an AI tool spent about two fewer hours per week on email and less time working after hours, but researchers did not detect a change in the amount or mix of tasks.
evidence_check.limit: The paper measures reported use and task exposure, not whether AI raised pay, reduced jobs or changed worker power. It is an early national measure, so later surveys may revise the picture.
evidence_check.location: Bick, Blandin, Deming and Schumacher, What Work Does Generative AI Do?, NBER Working Paper 35677, August 2026 abstract. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: The same job can contain different AI access
nodes.summary: Workers doing similar tasks may have different access to AI, training and permission to use it.
nodes.question: Who gets the tool, and who controls its use?
nodes.limit: Current evidence measures use, not yet the full effect on pay, job security or bargaining power.

evidence_check.title: Familiar speech may open more people-facing work
evidence_check.finding: An HBS account of research using Census, labor-market and audio records reports that the link between measured social skills and socially intensive work was at least 2.5 times stronger when workers spoke like the cultural group dominant in the workplace.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a manager may read familiarity as social skill, which can shape access to work where communication matters.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Speech, region, occupation and skill are linked in complex ways. The result is a group pattern, not proof that every hiring or promotion decision was biased.
evidence_check.limit: The HBS account does not provide a current employer-level hiring, promotion or pay audit. The audio and occupation measures also do not show what each manager heard or decided.
evidence_check.location: HBS Working Knowledge account of Workplace Communication as Systemic Disadvantage, HBS Working Paper 26-059. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Fit can decide who gets heard at work
nodes.summary: Communication style may shape access to people-facing work before a manager measures what a person can actually do.
nodes.question: When does familiarity look like skill?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence shows job sorting, not a full hiring, pay or promotion effect.

evidence_check.title: Years of work do not guarantee a higher career level
evidence_check.finding: An HBS account of an analysis of 150 million resumes and wage data reports that most workers reach a mid-level plateau. More than half of people with 10 years of work data had a seniority level of 10 or higher, but only 19% of those with 20 years of experience had reached a seniority level of 20.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: time at work and visible titles can hide how little real movement a person has made.
evidence_check.counterpoint: A worker may choose a stable role, change sectors, value flexibility, or gain pay without a higher title. A measured plateau is not automatically failure or harm.
evidence_check.limit: The measure does not by itself show job control, health, family security, or whether a worker wanted to advance. The current account does not connect career level to a later household choice.
evidence_check.location: HBS Working Knowledge account of NBER Working Paper 34292. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Work can continue while career movement slows
nodes.summary: Years on the job and a new title do not always mean more responsibility, pay or room for the next life choice.
nodes.question: What kind of progress did the worker actually gain?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures career level, not the worker's full economic or family result.

evidence_check.title: A financial stake worked better when the daily link was clear
evidence_check.finding: An HBS account of a field experiment at a 12-location building-materials company reports that concrete guidance about how daily behavior could affect equity value reduced turnover by 13 percentage points compared with broader values messaging. The difference grew during Hurricane Helene.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a distant ownership promise may change behavior only when workers can see how today's work connects to a possible payout.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Retention is not wealth or decision power. A stock claim can be delayed, uncertain or worthless, and workers may still have no say in company decisions.
evidence_check.limit: The study concerns one company, one equity plan and a short period. The current account does not show actual payouts, long-term wealth, effort, safety or governance power.
evidence_check.location: HBS Working Knowledge account of Making Equity Incentives Actionable, HBS Working Paper 26-085. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Ownership means little unless workers can see the link
nodes.summary: A financial claim may affect whether workers stay only when the company explains how daily work could create value for them.
nodes.question: What did the worker actually receive?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures retention, not payout, wealth or decision power.

evidence_check.title: A small shared office day changed later communication
evidence_check.finding: An NBER randomized trial of 248 customer-service employees reports 7.8% more calls per hour, 36 additional minutes of coworker communication after office visits, more manager feedback, and one-third lower attrition for workers assigned to attend the office together one day a month.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the useful part of an office day may be the relationships and feedback that continue after the day ends.
evidence_check.counterpoint: The trial concerns one multinational and workers within commuting distance. Fully remote work can reduce travel, widen hiring and help with care or health needs.
evidence_check.limit: The paper does not establish the best schedule for all jobs or workers, or whether communication gains become pay, promotion or worker control.
evidence_check.location: Aksoy, Bloom, Davis, Marino and Ozguzel, NBER Working Paper 35331, June 2026. Abstract checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: One office day can change the remote week
nodes.summary: A small shared meeting may matter because it creates communication and feedback that continue after workers go home.
nodes.question: What did the office day make possible later?
nodes.limit: The opening trial measures output, communication and retention, not worker preference, pay or promotion.

evidence_check.title: Low-income homes spend a larger share on energy
evidence_check.finding: The DOE LEAD tool reports an average energy burden of about 6% for low-income households and about 2% for non-low-income households. It also shows that burden can be much higher in some places.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the same energy price can leave different room for food, care, rent or debt because the bill takes a different share of income.
evidence_check.limit: These are modeled and survey-linked averages, not a bill for each household. Energy burden excludes transportation and does not by itself show a later cut in care, work or political trust.
evidence_check.location: US Department of Energy LEAD tool description and definition. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A home can be costly to heat before anything else changes
nodes.summary: Energy costs depend on income, building, fuel and place, so the same price can leave households with different room to adjust.
nodes.question: What does the energy bill crowd out?
nodes.limit: The opening packet measures burden, not the next household choice.

evidence_check.title: Getting to a place is a major household cost
evidence_check.finding: BLS reports that transportation averaged $13,318 per consumer unit in 2024, or 17.0% of spending. Vehicle-insurance spending rose 12.3% in 2024 after an 11.5% increase in 2023. Census reports a mean one-way commute of 27.2 minutes in 2024.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a household can pay for access through money and time. A cheaper home or job is not necessarily cheaper if the route between them is costly.
evidence_check.counterpoint: A costly trip can still buy access to a better job, school, store or care provider. Transportation spending is not automatically a loss; the next test must measure what the trip makes possible.
evidence_check.limit: These are national averages and a local-quality-of-life comparison. They do not show which households can switch modes, move closer or absorb a repair shock.
evidence_check.location: BLS Consumer Expenditure Surveys 2024 and Census 2024 commuting estimates. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Getting to a place is a major household cost
nodes.summary: Transportation can take money and time from the household before work, food, care or services begin.
nodes.question: What does the trip make possible, and what does it crowd out?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures spending and travel time, not the household's available alternatives.

evidence_check.title: A vehicle repair can arrive before the next paycheck
evidence_check.finding: NBER describes an unexpected car repair as a shock that can be hard to meet when savings are thin. Transportation spending and commute costs show why keeping a vehicle working can protect access to work and services.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a repair is not only a maintenance bill. For some households it may be a short deadline that tests cash, credit and the ability to reach a needed place.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Paying for a repair can preserve a job, a care visit or a food trip. The payment is not automatically a loss; the key question is what remains possible afterward.
evidence_check.limit: The opening sources do not follow the same US household from a repair to a missed trip, lost work, delayed bill or later debt.
evidence_check.location: NBER bill-timing digest, BLS 2024 consumer spending and NBER commuting-cost research. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A vehicle repair can arrive before the next paycheck
nodes.summary: A repair can test the household's cash buffer while protecting access to work, care and food.
nodes.question: What does a household give up to keep moving?
nodes.limit: The opening packet measures a plausible timing and access problem, not a proven job-loss effect.

evidence_check.title: Family help can move a shock between generations
evidence_check.finding: NBER reports that parents in lower-wealth households reduce financial help to adult children after adverse events, while children increase transfers and informal help to parents. HBS describes workers balancing care for children and aging parents with paid work.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: family support can keep a bill, job or care need covered while moving the cost to another person's cash, time or work room.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Family help can be fast, trusted and better suited to a need than a formal program. It may protect work and care rather than only hide a burden.
evidence_check.limit: The current sources do not follow both sides of one family around one event or show what the helper gives up afterward.
evidence_check.location: NBER family-support research and HBS caregiver reporting, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Family help can move a shock between generations
nodes.summary: Money and unpaid care can protect one household while using another household's room to act.
nodes.question: Who in the family catches the fall when money or health changes?
nodes.limit: The opening packet shows a family response, not a full measure of the cost or who lacks someone able to help.

evidence_check.title: A small business and its household can share one cash pool
evidence_check.finding: NBER's linked account data show a large business-revenue fall with a much smaller owner-consumption response during the pandemic. HBS reports linked data showing that college costs can affect both household spending and business investment.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: when family and business money are tied together, a shock may be absorbed by a choice that is hard to see in either a business-only or household-only report.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Holding household spending steady can protect the family and help the firm survive. Reducing business investment may be a sensible way to avoid a larger loss.
evidence_check.limit: The current US sources do not show which owners have another cash buffer or whether a household tradeoff later changes jobs, local services or business survival.
evidence_check.location: NBER linked-account research and HBS reporting on family-business cash flow, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A small business and its household can share one cash pool
nodes.summary: A business shock and a family bill can compete for the same money.
nodes.question: When money is tight, which side gets protected?
nodes.limit: The opening packet shows a linked cash-flow problem, not a proven effect on workers or local services.

evidence_check.title: More work does not always mean more room
evidence_check.finding: Recent NBER studies find that SNAP work requirements reduced participation among studied groups without increasing work. Federal analysis also models high effective loss rates as earnings rise across combinations of food, health, child care and cash programs.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a household may judge a raise by the help it loses and the costs it still must pay, not by the wage increase alone.
evidence_check.counterpoint: A gradual taper can let earnings replace aid while leaving a family better off. Program exit is not proof that total household resources fell.
evidence_check.limit: The current sources do not follow the same family's earnings, benefits, necessary costs and work choice across one change.
evidence_check.location: NBER SNAP work-requirement studies and US HHS benefit-cliff analysis, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: More work does not always mean more room
nodes.summary: A raise can change both pay and public help, so the household's real gain may be smaller or harder to predict.
nodes.question: What remains after earnings and lost help are counted together?
nodes.limit: The opening packet separates work rules, benefit loss and modeled rates; it does not yet measure one family's total resources.

evidence_check.title: A bill due date can become part of the energy burden
evidence_check.finding: An NBER research project uses private and linked administrative data to test whether the timing of utility bills against income changes late payment, service termination, credit scores and emergency-service outcomes. DOE's energy-burden measure shows why the same bill can leave different households with different room.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a household may be unable to pay not only because the bill is large, but because the money and due date do not line up.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Households may move a due date, use aid or pay before a shutoff. A late bill is not automatically a shutoff or a health event.
evidence_check.limit: The NBER project description names outcomes to study but does not establish a general estimate for every later health, credit or work effect.
evidence_check.location: NBER bill-timing research project and digest, with DOE energy-burden context. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A bill due date can become part of the energy burden
nodes.summary: The timing of income and utility bills may shape whether a household stays current and keeps service.
nodes.question: Can a timing mismatch become a service, credit or health problem?
nodes.limit: The opening packet identifies a testable mechanism but does not yet prove the full chain for all households.

evidence_check.title: Health coverage can hold a job in place
evidence_check.finding: NBER studies find that dependent coverage can increase parental job retention, and that losing public health coverage can increase job search and employment among people seeking employer coverage. Earlier work also found lower voluntary turnover among some workers with employer insurance and high medical expenses.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a job can be a wage and a route to care at the same time, so leaving may carry a cost that a wage comparison misses.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Employer coverage can be a valuable part of pay and can help a worker keep needed care. Staying is not proof of regret, poor job quality or lost opportunity.
evidence_check.limit: The current sources do not compare the full value of coverage with job quality, pay, family health needs and the next available plan for the same worker.
evidence_check.location: NBER dependent-coverage, employment-lock and job-mobility studies, with HBS health-care analysis. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Health coverage can hold a job in place
nodes.summary: A job can provide wages and health coverage together, making the cost of leaving hard to see.
nodes.question: How much of a job decision is really a health-coverage decision?
nodes.limit: The opening packet shows a coverage-related staying choice, not a general loss of mobility or well-being.

evidence_check.title: Removing medical debt can fix the record without fixing the illness
evidence_check.finding: Two randomized NBER experiments covering $169 million of medical debt for 83,401 people found modest credit-access improvement in one setting, lower payments on existing medical bills, and no average effect on surveyed health, health-care use or financial wellness.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: medical debt can mark a wider health and money shock. Removing the debt record may help one part of the chain while leaving the illness or care need in place.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Credit access is a real improvement and may matter for housing, borrowing or recovery. Average results can also hide effects for particular groups or kinds of debt.
evidence_check.limit: The experiment concerns downstream debt sold to collectors and selected relief programs; it does not cover every medical bill or show every household's later outcome.
evidence_check.location: NBER randomized medical-debt-relief experiments and HBS billing research, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Removing medical debt can fix the record without fixing the illness
nodes.summary: Debt relief may improve credit while leaving the health and care problem that produced the bill unchanged.
nodes.question: What does removing medical debt actually repair?
nodes.limit: The opening packet gives causal results for selected debt relief, not a general answer for every medical bill or patient.

evidence_check.title: Regular cash can change who can afford to live together
evidence_check.finding: An NBER study of low-income US parents found that the monthly 2021 Child Tax Credit was associated with changes in living arrangements, fewer people in the home, fewer expected moves caused by rent or mortgage trouble, and less back-owed housing payment.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: cash aid can create housing room to catch up, move, leave a financially necessary arrangement or reduce crowding.
evidence_check.counterpoint: A smaller household may mean needed independence or lost support. Staying together may be protective for one family and forced by money for another.
evidence_check.limit: The current study does not show that every living-arrangement change lasted or improved safety, care, work access or child well-being.
evidence_check.location: NBER Child Tax Credit housing study, unconditional cash-transfer study and HBS cash-and-agency reporting. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Regular cash can change who can afford to live together
nodes.summary: Cash aid can change housing payments and living arrangements, not only what a family buys.
nodes.question: What does regular cash allow a low-income family to change about its home?
nodes.limit: The opening packet measures housing and arrangement changes, not lasting well-being for every family.

evidence_check.title: A lost benefit can change how families read the economy
evidence_check.finding: An NBER study of the 2021 Child Tax Credit expiration estimates that each $1,000 in lost benefits reduced consumer sentiment by 1.7 points, with larger effects among lower-income families with multiple children; the effect persisted nearly two years.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: public policy can shape economic mood through a household's own lost room, not only through prices, interest rates or jobs.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Lower sentiment is not a changed vote or loss of trust. People may simply report feeling worse after a real income loss while keeping their work and longer plans unchanged.
evidence_check.limit: The current evidence does not connect the sentiment change to the same households' spending, trust, turnout or vote.
evidence_check.location: NBER Child Tax Credit sentiment study, housing study and HBS cash-and-control reporting. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A lost benefit can change how families read the economy
nodes.summary: A visible change in household cash can move public mood before it can be shown to change political behavior.
nodes.question: Can the loss of a household benefit change how people read the economy?
nodes.limit: The opening packet measures sentiment, not a changed vote, trust judgment or spending path.

evidence_check.title: Average income can hide an unsafe month
evidence_check.finding: NBER research links temporary income volatility to large welfare costs for low-liquidity households. Another NBER study finds that temporary workers face greater income risk and rationed credit, while HBS reports different spending patterns among people working multiple jobs despite comparable income.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a household can earn a similar amount over a year and still have less room if it cannot predict the next pay period.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Flexible or temporary work can offer entry, control or a higher upside. A household may accept risk because the alternative is worse.
evidence_check.limit: The current sources do not follow one worker's pay, cash buffer, credit terms and household choices through a specific job change.
evidence_check.location: NBER income-risk, credit and spending research, with HBS multiple-job spending evidence. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Average income can hide an unsafe month
nodes.summary: Unpredictable pay can change household choices even when annual income looks similar.
nodes.question: What does income risk do that an average wage misses?
nodes.limit: The opening packet links income risk to spending and credit conditions but does not prove one cause for every household.

evidence_check.title: A temporary payment can become a long monthly bill
evidence_check.finding: NBER estimates that households spent about 80% of a 2008 stimulus payment on durable goods within three months, mostly vehicles, and financed about 40 cents of each dollar of vehicle purchases with loans. HBS reports that installment checkout financing can raise spending and fees for some lower-income shoppers.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a one-time payment can improve access to a needed durable good while committing part of the future household budget.
evidence_check.counterpoint: A vehicle or appliance can protect work, care or daily life and may cost less than repeated repair or travel. Borrowing can be the sensible way to spread a necessary payment.
evidence_check.limit: The current sources do not follow the same household from purchase and loan terms through repayment, access and the next financial shock.
evidence_check.location: NBER durable-spending research and HBS installment-financing research, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A temporary payment can become a long monthly bill
nodes.summary: A large household purchase can improve daily access now while committing future cash.
nodes.question: What happens when a one-time payment meets a large household purchase?
nodes.limit: The opening packet shows purchase and financing responses, not the later effect on every household.

evidence_check.title: Cash can change the choices of people who did not receive it
evidence_check.finding: A recent randomized NBER guaranteed-income study finds that other household members became more likely to take part in education or training. It also finds more reports that someone in the household had forgone health care, a result the authors say may reflect greater engagement with care and newly identified unmet needs.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: regular cash can move time and decision power inside a household, helping one member act while making another person's unmet need more visible.
evidence_check.counterpoint: More reported forgone care is not proof that cash caused worse health. It may reflect better contact with care or awareness of a need that was already there.
evidence_check.limit: The current experiment does not show how household roles, health, work and debt change after payments end.
evidence_check.location: NBER guaranteed-income household and balance-sheet experiments, with HBS cash-and-control reporting. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Cash can change the choices of people who did not receive it
nodes.summary: A payment to one person can change training, care and spending decisions across the household.
nodes.question: What changes inside a household when only one person receives regular cash?
nodes.limit: The opening packet shows household spillovers, not a settled health or work effect after payments end.
subthemes: Cash, training and revealed care needs

evidence_check.title: New residents are workers and customers at once
evidence_check.finding: NBER estimates from US Census data that each immigrant created about 1.2 local jobs for local workers, mostly in non-traded services. Other research treats immigrants as both added labor supply and possible new business owners, while recent work finds roughly offsetting national supply and demand effects on inflation.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the local effect of migration depends on both the work people add and the services they buy, plus how fast housing and public systems adjust.
evidence_check.counterpoint: New demand can support local jobs, businesses and service variety. It can also add pressure where housing or public capacity expands slowly.
evidence_check.limit: The current sources do not show the same place's current housing, wages, services, belonging and political response together.
evidence_check.location: NBER local-demand, entrepreneurship and recent immigration research, with HBS migrant-local innovation reporting. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: New residents are workers and customers at once
nodes.summary: Migration can change a local economy through both the work people add and the services they need and buy.
nodes.question: What changes in a place when new residents add both workers and customers?
nodes.limit: The opening packet measures selected local and national effects, not the full experience of one place today.

evidence_check.title: A low first price can hide a higher choice
evidence_check.finding: NBER clickstream evidence shows that price obfuscation makes comparison harder and leads consumers to spend more than they otherwise would. HBS reports that no-fee intermediary pricing can still produce higher retail prices and unnecessary use of the intermediary.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the price a household can see and compare is part of the market outcome, not only a design detail.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Separate fees can reflect real service differences, and some shoppers value the intermediary or option. The key test is whether the full price is clear before commitment.
evidence_check.limit: The current sources do not show every shopper's final household cost, whether the purchase was unwanted or how the fee changed later trust or spending.
evidence_check.location: NBER price-salience and card-fee research, with HBS intermediary and price-format reporting. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A low first price can hide a higher choice
nodes.summary: Fees that appear late can change comparison, purchase and the amount a household pays.
nodes.question: What happens when the price seen is not the price paid?
nodes.limit: The opening packet measures choice and price display, not every household's later financial loss.

evidence_check.title: The way a person pays can change the price they carry
evidence_check.finding: NBER estimates that interchange fees transfer about $30 billion each year from cash and debit users to credit-card users, with consumer sorting and different merchant fees reducing but not removing the transfer. HBS explains how merchant fees can enter common prices while rewards return more value to premium-card users.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a payment product can redistribute money through ordinary shopping even when everyone sees the same shelf price.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Cards provide security, records, credit and rewards, and merchants may gain sales or lower handling costs. The full value of the payment method still has to be counted.
evidence_check.limit: The current sources do not show every household's actual price, reward, interest cost or ability to choose another merchant or payment method.
evidence_check.location: NBER payment-fee and card-fee research, with HBS payment-reward reporting. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: The way a person pays can change the price they carry
nodes.summary: Card fees and rewards can move money between shoppers through common prices.
nodes.question: Who pays when the same store accepts payment methods with different costs?
nodes.limit: The opening packet measures a redistribution mechanism, not every household's final net cost.

evidence_check.title: A payment record can become a gate to a home
evidence_check.finding: Linked Census and credit-bureau data show large differences in credit scores and serious delinquencies by race, class and hometown that emerge in young adulthood and persist. HBS reports that overdraft fees and unpaid balances can lead to account closure and a separate bank record.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a financial record can outlast the payment event and shape whether a person can borrow, rent or keep access to a bank account.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Records can help lenders price risk and extend credit to people who would otherwise be unknown. More data can help some people and expose others to harsher sorting.
evidence_check.limit: The current sources do not identify every cause of group gaps or show that one record alone caused a later housing or credit decision.
evidence_check.location: NBER credit-access and eviction research, with HBS overdraft and fintech reporting. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A payment record can become a gate to a home
nodes.summary: Credit visibility can open or close access to loans, housing and bank accounts long after a payment problem.
nodes.question: How does a financial record become a map of who can borrow or rent?
nodes.limit: The opening packet shows persistent group differences and gatekeeping risks, not one proven cause for every gap.
subthemes: Fees, account closure and housing access

evidence_check.title: An eviction order can narrow several choices at once
evidence_check.finding: Using linked administrative data and judge assignment, NBER finds that an eviction order increases homelessness and hospital visits and reduces earnings, durable-goods consumption and credit access in the first two years. Longer-run results include more debt and lower credit scores.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: an eviction can turn a housing problem into a work, health, spending and credit problem, while the earlier distress still matters.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Not every filing becomes an order, and legal help, payment plans or family support can prevent a move. A move can also be voluntary or improve a household's situation.
evidence_check.limit: The study covers two urban areas and shows distress before court, so the full later fall cannot be assigned to the order alone.
evidence_check.location: NBER eviction, credit and legal-representation research, with HBS rental-housing context. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: An eviction order can narrow several choices at once
nodes.summary: An eviction order can affect housing, work, health, spending and credit, but distress often starts before court.
nodes.question: What does an eviction order change beyond the loss of a home?
nodes.limit: The opening packet measures a causal order effect in selected cities, not the whole path for every tenant.
subthemes: Work, health and credit after eviction

evidence_check.title: A lawyer can stop a rent dispute from becoming a forced move
evidence_check.finding: NBER's study of New York City's Universal Access to Counsel rollout finds that tenants who gained legal representation were less likely to face possession judgments, had smaller money judgments, were less likely to receive eviction warrants and were less likely to be evicted. The effects were larger in poorer places and places with more noncitizens.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: access to a person who can answer in court may change the path before a housing problem becomes the wider eviction cascade.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Legal help does not erase unpaid rent, high housing costs or a landlord's claim. Results from one city program may not carry over to every court, tenant or form of aid.
evidence_check.limit: The study measures court and eviction outcomes in New York City; it does not show the full later path through work, health, credit or housing recovery.
evidence_check.location: Cassidy and Currie, The Effects of Legal Representation on Tenant Outcomes in Housing Court, NBER Working Paper 29836, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A lawyer can stop a rent dispute from becoming a forced move
nodes.summary: Legal representation can change a housing-court outcome before it becomes an eviction and a wider household loss.
nodes.question: Which problems can be prevented at the court door, and which remain after help arrives?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence is from one city program and does not measure the full household recovery path.

evidence_check.title: Rent aid can ease the bill without ending housing risk
evidence_check.finding: NBER's lottery-based study of emergency rental assistance in four US cities finds that aid increased rent payment and reduced concerns about eviction, with suggestive health gains, but had little overall effect on housing stability or financial distress. A separate study using landlord records finds that many tenants recover from missed payments and that broad prevention policies may have modest effects unless aimed at tenants likely to resume paying.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: money can relieve an immediate rent gap, but prevention depends on timing, the size of the gap, the landlord's choice and whether the household can keep paying later.
evidence_check.counterpoint: A short study period or an eviction moratorium may hide a real longer-term housing benefit. Aid can also prevent a crisis that would otherwise have been much worse even if it does not move the average housing-stability measure.
evidence_check.limit: The studies cover selected programs and rental markets; they do not identify one national best design or follow every household after assistance ends.
evidence_check.location: NBER emergency rental assistance and nonpayment research, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Rent aid can ease the bill without ending housing risk
nodes.summary: Rental assistance can improve immediate payment and reduce fear while leaving the deeper housing problem in place.
nodes.question: When does rent aid prevent displacement, and when does it only buy time?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence does not establish one national design or the lasting path after assistance ends.

evidence_check.title: Keeping a home may protect the next job
evidence_check.finding: NBER links callers to a Chicago homelessness-prevention hotline with federal tax records and uses quasi-random funding availability to compare similar families. Looking up to four years later, it finds evidence of employment and earnings gains, especially for the lowest earners, and no evidence that short-term assistance lowers work or earnings.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: emergency help may protect work capacity by keeping a housing crisis from taking over the next job decision.
evidence_check.counterpoint: The study concerns people who reached one Chicago hotline and received short-term help. Higher later earnings may reflect who could use the help or other changes around the crisis, even with the study's comparison design.
evidence_check.limit: The evidence does not show which housing event was prevented, whether the person kept the same job, or how the result changes across places and aid designs.
evidence_check.location: Hungerman, Phillips, Rinz and Sullivan, The Effect of Emergency Financial Assistance on Employment and Earnings, NBER Working Paper 32856, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Keeping a home may protect the next job
nodes.summary: Short-term help during a housing crisis may protect employment and later earnings, especially for the lowest earners.
nodes.question: Does preventing a housing break protect work, or does work recover for another reason?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence follows one Chicago hotline population and does not identify the full housing event or job path.

evidence_check.title: Rent insurance could move a short shock away from the tenant
evidence_check.finding: NBER models rent-guarantee insurance that makes a limited number of payments to a landlord when an insured tenant cannot pay after an income or health shock. The model finds welfare gains, smaller security deposits and less homelessness, but says unrestricted private or public access is not financially viable. Private insurers would target better-off renters, while public insurance would need to focus on households most at risk.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the design of protection decides whether a product shares risk or leaves the households most likely to need it outside the market.
evidence_check.counterpoint: This is a model, not evidence from a broad US insurance rollout. A product could also add a premium, exclusions or a new screening rule that changes who can rent.
evidence_check.limit: The study does not measure actual tenant take-up, claims, premiums, landlord behavior or later credit and housing outcomes.
evidence_check.location: Abramson and Van Nieuwerburgh, Rent Guarantee Insurance, NBER Working Paper 32582, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Rent insurance could move a short shock away from the tenant
nodes.summary: Rent-guarantee insurance may share a short payment shock, but market design may exclude the households most at risk.
nodes.question: Who can buy protection before a rent shock, and who is left with the loss?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence is a model and does not show actual take-up, claims or later household outcomes.

evidence_check.title: Insurance risk can become a home and credit problem
evidence_check.finding: NBER research using mortgage-linked insurance records finds that property premiums rose sharply from 2020 to 2023, with larger increases in places facing more disaster risk, and that higher premiums were reflected in slower home-price growth in exposed ZIP codes. A newer NBER study reports that credit scores affect homeowners-insurance premiums alongside disaster risk.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the cost of keeping a home may now depend on both the place's physical risk and the owner's financial record, tightening the link between insurance, credit and housing choice.
evidence_check.counterpoint: A premium reflects expected loss and insurer pricing, not a complete measure of what a household can afford. Home prices, building changes, state rules and the ability to self-insure may alter the effect.
evidence_check.limit: The studies do not show whether a specific household dropped coverage, lost a mortgage, moved or reduced other spending because of the premium.
evidence_check.location: Keys and Mulder, Property Insurance and Disaster Risk, NBER Working Paper 32579; Weill, Pricing Protection, NBER Working Paper 34848. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Insurance risk can become a home and credit problem
nodes.summary: Home insurance prices can connect disaster exposure and credit standing to the cost and value of staying in a home.
nodes.question: When does keeping a home protected become a new barrier to keeping the home?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures premiums and market values, not the same household's full payment and move decisions.

evidence_check.title: Working from home can change what a household buys and pays
evidence_check.finding: NBER's 2026 study finds that working from home increased online shopping, weekday store trips, total spending, product quantity and range, and spending on food and general merchandise. It also finds higher prices paid, less use of deals and lower price sensitivity, with price changes concentrated among married households as shopping responsibility shifted, especially when the remote worker was male.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: remote work changes the household's shopping system, not only the location of the job. The time saved from commuting may be exchanged for more quantity, more convenience or less deal hunting.
evidence_check.counterpoint: More shopping and higher spending can reflect better access, more choice or useful convenience. The study does not show that higher prices made households worse off, or that the shopping shift was unwanted.
evidence_check.limit: The current evidence does not show the same household's time value, income, product need, final welfare or longer-run division of unpaid work.
evidence_check.location: Baker, Bloom, Johnson and Obradović, Shopping From Home, NBER Working Paper 34883, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Working from home can change what a household buys and pays
