nodes.summary: Remote work can alter shopping time, product choice, prices paid and who carries the household shopping job.
nodes.question: When work moves home, who gains time and who takes on the shopping system?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence shows shopping changes but not whether the household is better off after time, price and unpaid work are counted together.

evidence_check.title: A power outage can turn payment choice into a basic access problem
evidence_check.finding: NBER's 2026 study combines outage, weather, transaction, scanner and survey data from the United States and other countries. It finds that spending rises before disasters as households stock up, often using credit; after outages, digital payments fall and cash use rises. Nearly half of surveyed consumers could not use their preferred electronic payment during an outage, and greater cash access reduced the drop in completed purchases.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a payment system is part of household infrastructure. When electricity or networks fail, cash is not just an old preference; it can decide whether a person can complete a necessary purchase.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Cash also brings theft, loss and access problems, and outages differ by place and length. Offline-capable cards or other tools may provide resilience without requiring people to hold much cash.
evidence_check.limit: The study does not show which households lose food, medicine, fuel or work access, or which payment design works best for every outage.
evidence_check.location: Alvarez, Argente and Van Patten, On the Resilience of Payment Methods, NBER Working Paper 35115, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A power outage can turn payment choice into a basic access problem
nodes.summary: When digital payment fails, cash access can decide whether households complete purchases after a disaster.
nodes.question: What can a household still buy when the payment network goes down?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence shows payment and spending changes, not the full effect on food, medicine, fuel or work.

evidence_check.title: Well-timed credit can keep a disaster from becoming bankruptcy
evidence_check.finding: NBER links US Federal Disaster Loan applications to credit records and uses an approval cutoff to compare similar applicants. It finds that approved emergency credit reduced the likelihood of bankruptcy by 61% over the following three years, with additional car purchases even three years later. The evidence points to liquidity—the ability to pay at the right time—as the main channel.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: credit can be protective when it arrives after a shock and before missed bills compound. The timing and terms matter more than approval alone.
evidence_check.counterpoint: The loans covered uninsured damage after federally declared disasters and were available to applicants who reached the program. The result may not apply to ordinary high-interest consumer credit or households that cannot qualify.
evidence_check.limit: The study does not show the loan's full cost, which household need was preserved, or whether the later car purchase improved or strained household finances.
evidence_check.location: Collier, Hartley, Keys and Ng, Credit When You Need It, NBER Working Paper 32845, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Well-timed credit can keep a disaster from becoming bankruptcy
nodes.summary: Emergency credit can reduce severe financial distress after a disaster when it arrives early enough and on workable terms.
nodes.question: When does borrowing protect a household, and when does it only move the loss forward?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence concerns a federal disaster-loan program and does not describe ordinary consumer credit or every household's need.

evidence_check.title: Emergency business credit can keep local work alive
evidence_check.finding: NBER's study of government recovery loans after US natural disasters finds that the loans reduced small-business exit and bankruptcy, increased employment and revenue, unlocked private credit and reduced delinquency. The authors link the effects partly to resolving uncertainty about whether repairs could be completed and find some positive spillovers on local business entry.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: disaster liquidity can protect more than the owner's firm. It may preserve jobs, local services and the next business that depends on the damaged firm remaining open.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Government credit may keep a weak firm alive or shift risk to taxpayers and lenders. The study finds no capital reallocation away from nearby firms, but local customer and worker effects still need close measurement.
evidence_check.limit: The study does not show the owner's household spending, the quality of preserved jobs or which local customers lose access when a firm exits.
evidence_check.location: Collier, Howell and Rendell, After the Storm: How Emergency Liquidity Helps Small Businesses Following Natural Disasters, NBER Working Paper 32326, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Emergency business credit can keep local work alive
nodes.summary: Recovery loans can reduce small-business exit while protecting employment, revenue and local economic links after a disaster.
nodes.question: When a small firm survives a shock, who else keeps their options?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures firm outcomes, not the full owner, worker, customer or neighborhood path.

evidence_check.title: A bigger small-business rule can squeeze the smallest firms
evidence_check.finding: A new NBER study uses Census administrative data and changes in US small-business program eligibility. It finds that expanding access to larger firms reduced revenue for the smallest firms, especially younger, more productive and financially constrained firms. Government contracts moved toward larger firms, while exits rose and wages and patenting fell.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a support program can look broad while shifting opportunity away from the firms with the least cash and the most growth potential.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Larger firms may be able to deliver at scale, meet procurement needs or support more workers. The study concerns particular eligibility changes and does not mean every larger-firm award harms smaller firms.
evidence_check.limit: The opening paper does not show each owner's household result, customer prices, local service loss or which program design would best balance scale and access.
evidence_check.location: Brown, Denes, Duchin and Hackney, How Big is Small? The Economic Effects of Access to Small Business Government Support, NBER Working Paper 35703, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A bigger small-business rule can squeeze the smallest firms
nodes.summary: Changing the size rule for public support can shift contracts, revenue, exits, wages and innovation between firms.
nodes.question: Who gains when a program called small-business support reaches larger firms?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures firm and market outcomes, not the full owner, worker, customer or local-service effect.

evidence_check.title: A promise about debt can change spending before the rule is settled
evidence_check.finding: NBER's US study of the 2022 student-loan-forgiveness promise uses an information experiment linked to credit, employment and spending records. Borrowers more optimistic about forgiveness paid about $40 less per month on student loans and spent about $80 more per month on nondurables. Borrowers optimistic about payment pauses were 7.5 percentage points more likely to be delinquent after payments resumed. The authors' model says overly optimistic beliefs could cost up to 6.9% of the starting balance.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: policy uncertainty is itself a household financial condition. A promise can change the budget before any money is cancelled, and a later reversal can turn delayed payment into delinquency.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Borrowers may have used the extra spending for needed goods or may have made a reasonable choice while the policy was being litigated. The modeled balance cost is not a direct loss for every borrower.
evidence_check.limit: The study does not show how beliefs formed outside the experiment, which household need received the extra spending, or the full political and family effects of uncertainty.
evidence_check.location: Koustas, Weber and Yannelis, Beliefs and Actions under Government Policy Uncertainty, NBER Working Paper 35319, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A promise about debt can change spending before the rule is settled
nodes.summary: Uncertain forgiveness or payment rules can change loan payments, spending and later delinquency before policy is final.
nodes.question: What does a policy promise make households do before the promise becomes real?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures one US student-loan episode and does not show every household's need, belief source or later welfare.

evidence_check.title: People may hear the same economic message differently by party
evidence_check.finding: NBER's survey experiment with 5,205 US consumers finds that people who see the Federal Reserve as politically aligned with them report more trust, are more likely to receive or pay for its communications, and give its messages more weight when updating inflation expectations. The study finds strong in-group effects, while overall trust can stay steady as its partisan composition changes.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: public trust is not only a view of whether prices are rising. It also affects whether people accept the institution's explanation of what happens next.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Trust and belief responses in a survey do not show actual spending, borrowing or voting. People may judge the Fed through the president, tariffs, personal finances or media rather than the institution's own message.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not show whether a change in trust changes household action or how durable the communication effect is outside an experiment.
evidence_check.location: Kuang, Weber and Xie, Perceived Political Bias of the Federal Reserve, NBER Working Paper 33071; Binder, Couture and Smit, Partisan Trust in the Federal Reserve, NBER Working Paper 33684. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: People may hear the same economic message differently by party
nodes.summary: Perceived political alignment can change trust in the Fed and how much weight households give its inflation message.
nodes.question: When does an economic message become a test of who people think is on their side?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures trust and belief updates, not later spending, voting or policy demand.

evidence_check.title: The same price rise can produce different blame
evidence_check.finding: NBER's US survey and information experiments find that people see inflation as broadly negative and often name government actions, production costs, firms, oil, supply chains or recent events as causes. Party registration and news sources shape those attributions. Many respondents also understate the tradeoffs involved in fighting inflation and support policies that may conflict with their own stated theory of the problem.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a price shock becomes political through a story about who caused it and what should be done, not through the price number alone.
evidence_check.counterpoint: People may have good reasons for using different examples: their bills, local news and personal exposure differ. A survey answer about causes does not show later blame, voting or policy action.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence is survey-based and does not link one person's price basket, information source, economic loss and political action over time.
evidence_check.location: Binetti, Nuzzi and Stantcheva, People's Understanding of Inflation, NBER Working Paper 32497, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: The same price rise can produce different blame
nodes.summary: People's explanation of inflation varies by party and news source, shaping which policy response sounds reasonable.
nodes.question: How does a household price become a story about responsibility and action?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures beliefs and policy preferences, not the same person's later vote or household behavior.

evidence_check.title: Bad price news can weigh more than good price news
evidence_check.finding: NBER's household-panel study finds that news coverage is more likely when inflation is high and that households account for this pattern imperfectly. Exposure to news about higher prices raises inflation expectations by 0.4 percentage point, while exposure to lower-price news has no significant effect.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the public picture of the economy can lean negative because the news people see is selected around bad price movements, and the correction is not equal when prices improve.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Higher-price news may contain information people need, and lower-price news may be less common because falling prices are less newsworthy. A change in expectations is not the same as a change in spending or voting.
evidence_check.limit: The studies do not show each household's complete media diet, price basket, trust, spending response or political action.
evidence_check.location: Chahrour, Shapiro and Wilson, News Selection and Household Inflation Expectations, NBER Working Paper 33837; Binder, Frank and Ryngaert, The Causal Effect of News on Inflation Expectations, NBER Working Paper 34088. Checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Bad price news can weigh more than good price news
nodes.summary: The selection and timing of inflation news can make household expectations respond more to higher prices than lower ones.
nodes.question: How does the news people receive shape the economic future they expect?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures news exposure and inflation expectations, not later household or political action.

evidence_check.title: Future public debt can change what households expect before taxes change
evidence_check.finding: A randomized NBER study of US households finds that information about current debt or deficits has little effect on inflation expectations, while information about future debt leads households to expect higher future inflation, spending and government borrowing costs. The response is to the future fiscal path, not simply to today's debt number.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a government plan can enter household decisions before a tax, benefit or interest-rate change arrives, because people act on what they think the future bill will be.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Expectations are not spending records, and a household may understand future debt differently from an economist. The study does not show who changes a budget or political view after receiving the information.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not show the same household's income, debt exposure, spending, saving, political response or later realized fiscal policy.
evidence_check.location: Coibion, Gorodnichenko and Weber, Fiscal Policy and Households' Inflation Expectations, NBER Working Paper 28485, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Future public debt can change what households expect before taxes change
nodes.summary: Information about future public debt can change household expectations about inflation, spending and government borrowing before policy reaches the budget.
nodes.question: When does a future public bill change today's household choice?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence measures expectations, not the same household's later spending, saving or political action.

evidence_check.title: A public water fix can become a health and place benefit
evidence_check.finding: A new NBER study uses decades of water tests from 48 states and Medicare records for older Americans. It finds that readings above current health standards fell by about half from 2003 to 2019, that low-income areas had higher pollution, and that Safe Drinking Water Act loans reduced pollution and older-adult mortality. The authors estimate that removing pollution above health standards could cost about $46 per person a year at the average loan cost.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: water quality is not only an environmental measure. It can change health risk and the value people receive from a public system, with the burden still falling unevenly across places.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Pollution has fallen, and the study's loan estimates do not mean every system needs the same spending. Black and Hispanic community patterns are mixed, and a water test does not by itself show each household's exposure or response.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not follow the same household through water exposure, bottled-water spending, health care, home value, trust or political action.
evidence_check.location: Keiser, Mazumder, Molitor and Shapiro, Water Works: Causes and Consequences of Safe Drinking Water in America, NBER Working Paper 35288, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A public water fix can become a health and place benefit
nodes.summary: Water quality links public investment to health, household trust and the value of living in a place, with unequal exposure still visible.
nodes.question: When does a basic public service change both health and what a place is worth to the people living there?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures water pollution, loans and older-adult mortality, not the full household cost or political path.

evidence_check.title: A fee rule can help people with cash more than people without it
evidence_check.finding: An NBER study of large US banks finds that removing non-sufficient-funds fees cut those charges across income groups. Relaxing overdraft rules reduced overdraft fees mainly for wealthier and more liquid households; only those households later had lower late fees, interest payments, account fees and payday-loan use. The changes did not substantially reduce financial stress among the most vulnerable households.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: equal-looking bank relief can have unequal value because the starting cash position decides whether a person can avoid the next cost.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Removing a fee is still a direct gain, and overdraft access may stop a payment from failing. The study does not say that every lower-income customer was worse off or that every alternative product was used after an overdraft.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not follow the same household from the bill that caused the shortage through payment success, later cost, housing, health or trust.
evidence_check.location: Pagel, Sridhar and Williams, Bank Fees and Household Financial Well-Being, NBER Working Paper 34993, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A fee rule can help people with cash more than people without it
nodes.summary: Bank fee changes can remove a charge while leaving the households with the least cash exposed to later costs.
nodes.question: When does a bank rule create real room rather than move the shortage somewhere else?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures account fees and later financial products, not the full household result.

evidence_check.title: A score can help cause the default it predicts
evidence_check.finding: An NBER study finds that an extra counted credit inquiry lowers scores by about five points without changing the credit report. Default does not change for consumers with clean records, but rises by 3.2 percentage points over two years for consumers with prior derogatory marks. At least 13% of the score-default link for that group appears self-fulfilling.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a financial record can become part of the event it is meant to measure when a lower score makes the next loan harder or more costly.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Scores can help lenders sort risk and may protect borrowers from loans they cannot repay. This result concerns a defined higher-risk group and does not show that removing scores would improve outcomes.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not show which lender decision caused the default or the same borrower's later housing, work, insurance or score-recovery path.
evidence_check.location: Duarte and Fonseca, Self-Fulfilling Credit Scores, NBER Working Paper 35508, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A score can help cause the default it predicts
nodes.summary: For people with damaged credit records, a score change that adds no new household fact may still raise the chance of default.
nodes.question: When does a record become a barrier that helps produce the result it forecasts?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures score movement and default for a defined group, not the full household and housing path.

evidence_check.title: Automatic saving can grow an account and a credit-card balance
evidence_check.finding: An NBER comparison of private-sector workers likely exposed to Oregon's automatic-enrollment IRA with workers in states that had not adopted one finds increases in checking or savings account ownership and balances, along with higher credit-card debt.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a workplace saving rule can strengthen one part of a household balance sheet while adding pressure somewhere else. Account growth alone does not tell us whether the household has more room.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Credit-card debt is not automatically a loss if new savings are more liquid, replace a costlier loan, or help a person handle a shock. Automatic saving may reach workers who would not open an account on their own.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not show whether the added savings are liquid, why debt rose, how take-home pay changed, or whether retirement security improved later.
evidence_check.location: Bloomfield, Dao, Lee and Slavov, How Do State Auto-IRA Policies Affect Household Balance Sheets?, NBER Working Paper 35373, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Automatic saving can grow an account and a credit-card balance
nodes.summary: A state workplace-saving rule can increase account ownership and balances while also raising credit-card debt.
nodes.question: Does automatic saving create a buffer, or does it move short-term pressure into another account?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures balance-sheet changes, not the full tradeoff between current room and later security.

evidence_check.title: The same spending number can hide different constraints
evidence_check.finding: An NBER study using transaction records and survey expectations for middle-income US consumers with little liquid wealth finds large and varied gaps between observed spending and a no-friction benchmark. The median gap is 40% of the benchmark in absolute value; 49% of consumers spend below it and 51% above it. Borrowing limits alone cannot explain both directions. The patterns fit a mix of cash limits, present focus and the cost of changing consumption.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: lower or higher spending does not tell us by itself whether people wanted that result. Cash, credit and the cost of changing a plan can sit underneath the visible purchase.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Spending above or below a model benchmark is not automatically a mistake. People may have real needs or a good reason to value today more than later, and the benchmark cannot decide that alone.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not show which purchase changed, whether the change helped or harmed the household, or the later food, care, housing or debt result.
evidence_check.location: Indarte, Kluender, Malmendier and Stepner, Consumption Wedges: Measuring and Diagnosing Distortions, NBER Working Paper 34891, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: The same spending number can hide different constraints
nodes.summary: Observed consumer spending can reflect cash limits, credit limits, future focus or the cost of changing course, not just preference.
nodes.question: What is underneath the purchase number?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures model-based spending gaps, not the full household outcome behind them.

evidence_check.title: More income risk at the top can mean more saving and wider wealth gaps
evidence_check.finding: Using newly digitized US tax returns from 1969 to 2019, an NBER study finds that permanent income risk rose across the distribution and nearly 70% among the top 5%. Large negative income shocks predict financial distress even among top earners. A life-cycle model links higher risk at the top to more saving, greater wealth inequality and a 0.7 percentage-point reduction in the modeled risk-free rate.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a change among high earners can affect the wider economy through saving and the price of money, even though the first shock is far from an ordinary checkout or rent payment.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Higher saving can fund investment and provide protection against a shock. The modeled wealth and interest-rate effects depend on assumptions and do not show the same result for every household.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not show how the change reaches consumers, workers, borrowers or voters, and the tax records do not explain each saving decision.
evidence_check.location: Braxton, Herkenhoff, Huang, Nattinger, Rothbaum and Schmidt, Rising Income Risk at the Top, NBER Working Paper 35664, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: More income risk at the top can mean more saving and wider wealth gaps
nodes.summary: Rising income risk among high earners may change saving, wealth and the price of money beyond the households first hit.
nodes.question: When does a change at the top reach the financial room of other households?

evidence_check.title: A dominant employer may carry local job power into politics
evidence_check.finding: An NBER study finds that workers at major local employers are more likely to report employer political communication and to say their employer influences their voting behavior and career expectations. Its model describes passive and active paths through which a dominant employer shapes expectations about wages and jobs after an election.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a job can shape political judgment through dependence and future expectations, not only through the paycheck received today.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Workers may hear an employer's view without accepting it, and a large employer can provide stable jobs or useful local information. Reported influence is not proof of a changed vote.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not show the same worker's message, job dependence, belief change and vote in one record.
evidence_check.location: Avenancio-León, Barbalau, Hou and Piccolo, Firms as Electoral Monopsonies, NBER Working Paper 35676, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A dominant employer may carry local job power into politics
nodes.summary: A major local employer may shape political expectations through the worker's dependence on the job and the firm's message about the future.
nodes.question: When does workplace power become political power?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures reported influence and a model, not the same worker's later vote.

evidence_check.title: The same income can buy a different life by place
evidence_check.finding: An NBER study using household consumption data covering about 5% of the US population and local prices for more than 140 products finds that price differences between commuting zones are especially large for low-income households. The spatial spread of low-income price indexes is almost twice the spread for high-income households.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a national income number can hide a local customer reality. Where a family lives can change how much of its paycheck remains after ordinary purchases.
evidence_check.counterpoint: High prices may come with better jobs, services or amenities, while low prices may come with fewer choices. A price index alone is not a complete measure of a place's value.
evidence_check.limit: The opening result does not show why households stay, move, change stores, change products, or experience the local price as a better or worse life.
evidence_check.location: Diamond and Moretti, Where is Standard of Living the Highest? Local Prices and the Geography of Consumption, NBER Working Paper 29533, revised May 2026, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: The same income can buy a different life by place
nodes.summary: Local prices can change the real room left by a paycheck, especially for lower-income households.
nodes.question: What does a family's income actually buy where it lives?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures local prices and consumption, not the full move, service or household well-being path.

evidence_check.title: Public help can change how families see the economy
evidence_check.finding: An NBER study using monthly University of Michigan consumer-sentiment data and differences in likely Child Tax Credit loss finds that the policy affected perceived economic well-being beyond the change in current income. The authors point to possible effects on household activity, political attitudes and voting.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a public benefit can change the story a family tells about its financial position, not only the money in its account.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Families judge the economy from many prices, jobs and news stories. A benefit can change sentiment without changing long-run finances or political behavior.
evidence_check.limit: The opening result does not show the same family's spending, saving, policy support or vote after the benefit changed.
evidence_check.location: Bastian and Harvey, When Policy Shapes Perception: The 2021 Child Tax Credit and Consumer Sentiment, NBER Working Paper 35059, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Public help can change how families see the economy
nodes.summary: A benefit or benefit loss may change personal and national economic feeling beyond the direct income change.
nodes.question: When does public help become part of how people judge the economy and government?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures perceived economic well-being, not the same family's later spending or vote.

evidence_check.title: Beliefs about who pays can change which policy wins
evidence_check.finding: An NBER study finds that respondents think market-based environmental tools raise consumer energy bills more than standards do, unlike expert environmental economists. Its model shows that political limits and imperfect cost beliefs can push policy toward a less cost-effective standard.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the expected household bill can shape public policy before the actual bill or environmental result is known.
evidence_check.counterpoint: People may care about fairness, control and trust, not only total cost. A standard can be easier to understand or enforce even if another tool looks more efficient to an economist.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not show each household's actual bill, policy knowledge, pollution result or later political action.
evidence_check.location: Shapiro and Taubinsky, Understanding Support for Cost-Ineffective Environmental Policy Instruments, NBER Working Paper 35073, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Beliefs about who pays can change which policy wins
nodes.summary: Expected energy costs can shape support for environmental rules before people see the actual bill or result.
nodes.question: When does a consumer cost belief change public policy?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures beliefs and a model of policy choice, not the full household bill or environmental result.

evidence_check.title: Two apps can show different prices while customers still compare rarely
evidence_check.finding: An NBER audit of 2,238 matched New York City trips found an average absolute price gap of about $3.50, or roughly 14% of the average fare. Device data show that only about 16% of people who opened one app also opened the other, even though neither app was consistently cheaper.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a market can look competitive while many customers see only one price. App habit and the effort of checking can leave bargaining power with the platform.
evidence_check.counterpoint: People may value wait time, reliability, discounts, account history or habit more than the lowest fare. A higher price can buy a better service or save time.
evidence_check.limit: The study covers one city and a short price window. It does not show each rider's income, reason for choosing an app, service quality, final cost or later switching.
evidence_check.location: Fossett, Luca and Xu, Leaving Money on the Dashboard: Price Dispersion and Search Frictions on Uber and Lyft, NBER Working Paper 34441; NBER Digest checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Two apps can show different prices while customers still compare rarely
nodes.summary: Rideshare customers may leave money unclaimed when app habit and search effort keep them from checking both platforms.
nodes.question: When does convenience weaken customer price power?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures matched fares and app opening, not each rider's full value or switching reason.

evidence_check.title: A license rule may not improve the ride customers receive
evidence_check.finding: An NBER study using trip-level Uber ratings and telematics-based driving measures finds no consistent evidence that occupational licensing improves consumer outcomes in its New York, New Jersey and Houston settings. In Houston, drivers entering after deregulation looked like previously licensed drivers on ratings and driving behavior despite differences in age and experience.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a rule described as customer protection may mainly change who can enter the work unless the service result is measured directly.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Licensing may protect customers through checks or standards not captured by ratings and the driving measures used here. It may also matter more under different enforcement or in other cities.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not show fares, wait times, worker income, entry costs or every safety outcome, and results from two settings may not carry to all cities.
evidence_check.location: Hall, Hicks, Kleiner and Oh, Occupational Licensing of Uber Drivers, NBER Working Paper 35635, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A license rule may not improve the ride customers receive
nodes.summary: Rideshare licensing may change worker entry without a clear measured gain in ratings or driving behavior for customers.
nodes.question: When does a customer-protection rule improve the service rather than narrow access to the work?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures ratings and driving behavior in selected settings, not the full fare, safety or worker path.

evidence_check.title: Equal data access can open competition and reduce data investment
evidence_check.finding: An NBER model studies rules that require a platform to treat affiliated and outside sellers equally when sharing data. Equal data amounts can be weakened by discriminatory data prices. Equal data and prices open competition more, but may reduce the platform's reason to improve or produce data, so customer welfare need not rise in every case.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a platform can be both the market gate and the maker of the information used in the market. Opening the gate may change the quality of the information too.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Without equal access, a platform may favor its own sellers and keep rivals weak. A reduction in data investment may be small if the platform has other reasons to improve the service.
evidence_check.limit: The opening source is a model and does not test a named US platform rule, actual seller prices, data quality or customer outcomes.
evidence_check.location: Fang and Kim, Data Neutrality, Data Supply, and Market Competition, NBER Working Paper 35159, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Equal data access can open competition and reduce data investment
nodes.summary: A rule that opens platform data to outside sellers may improve competition while changing how much useful data the platform produces.
nodes.question: When does a data fairness rule help customers, and when does it weaken the information they need?
nodes.limit: The opening source is a model, not a measured result from a named US platform.

evidence_check.title: A platform-owned product can help some customers and still raise competition concerns
evidence_check.finding: In a field experiment that hid Amazon-owned brands from shoppers, an NBER study finds that customers chose similar products without more search or cross-platform switching. Some customers preferred Amazon brands, and removing them reduced estimated consumer welfare by 5.5%. Moving the brands lower in search did not raise welfare because prominent placement was valuable to some customers.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: platform control can create a real conflict while the platform's own product still fits some customers better. Short-run customer benefit and long-run seller competition need separate tests.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Self-preferencing can make it harder for outside sellers to grow even when some customers like the platform product. A field result in one product setting does not settle the wider market effect.
evidence_check.limit: The opening study does not show long-run seller entry, prices, platform investment, or whether the result carries to other product groups and platforms.
evidence_check.location: Farronato, Fradkin and MacKay, Vertical Integration and Consumer Choice: Evidence from a Field Experiment, NBER Working Paper 34135, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A platform-owned product can help some customers and still raise competition concerns
nodes.summary: A platform-owned product can serve a real customer preference while the platform's control over search remains a competition question.
nodes.question: When does a platform's own product help customers, and when does it close the market?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures short-run choice and estimated welfare in one platform setting, not long-run competition.

evidence_check.title: A free service can have time as its real price
evidence_check.finding: Using two field experiments on Facebook and Instagram, an NBER study finds that users respond only a little to ad load, the main user cost in the setting. The share of a person's time devoted to an activity and the cost of that time affect which other online or offline activities can replace it. The paper also models the possible effect of separating the two platforms.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: a service can be costly through time and attention even when no money changes hands. Competition should count the time price, not only the subscription price.
evidence_check.counterpoint: People may stay because the service is valuable, familiar or socially important. More ads can be a tolerable price for a service that remains free, and time spent is not automatically time lost.
evidence_check.limit: The opening evidence does not show long-run well-being, the value of each activity, household care or work effects, or the result of an actual separation.
evidence_check.location: Goodman, de Frahan, Holz, List, MacMenamin, McKay, Mogstad, Sadoff and Sider, Consumer Demand and Market Competition with Time-Intensive Goods, NBER Working Paper 34743, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A free service can have time as its real price
nodes.summary: Online services may compete through the time and attention they take, not only through a money price.
nodes.question: What does a free service really cost the customer?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures time use and ad response, not the full household or well-being result.

evidence_check.title: A tariff can reach US prices later through domestic markups
evidence_check.finding: Studying the 2025 US tariffs, an NBER study estimates that about 26% of the tariff increase passed through to consumer prices relative to less-exposed goods. About 64% of that increase was direct, while 36% came indirectly through imported inputs and higher domestic markups as imports became less competitive. The direct effect was quick; the indirect effect took about nine to twelve months.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: the consumer effect of a trade policy may keep building after the first shelf-price jump because domestic firms face higher inputs and less import competition.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Domestic firms may use the pressure to invest, switch suppliers or expand production. A higher price can also reflect a change in product mix or demand, not only a tariff.
evidence_check.limit: The estimate is relative to less-exposed goods and holds aggregate conditions fixed. It does not show the exact household bill, jobs, firm entry or the full long-run response.
evidence_check.location: Amiti, Heise and Weinstein, The Anatomy of Tariff Pass-through into Consumer Prices, NBER Working Paper 35561, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: A tariff can reach US prices later through domestic markups
nodes.summary: Tariffs can affect consumer prices directly and later through imported inputs and less import competition for US producers.
nodes.question: Why can the household price effect keep growing after the tariff starts?
nodes.limit: The opening study measures product-price paths, not the full household, job or political result.

evidence_check.title: Competition can protect the customers most able to leave
evidence_check.finding: Using nationwide data from three US industries before the 1964 Civil Rights Act, an NBER study finds that increases in non-discrimination were concentrated in the least competitive markets, where the threat of White customer defection was lowest. Non-discriminatory firms charged higher prices than discriminatory firms in the same local market, and Black customers were harmed through higher prices in the non-discriminatory market.
evidence_check.meaning: Working interpretation: competition does not automatically protect every customer. Firms may respond most strongly to the group with the clearest ability to leave.
evidence_check.counterpoint: Competition can still discipline firms and open better options when customers can switch. A higher price may reflect a different service or cost, not discrimination alone.
evidence_check.limit: This is historical evidence and does not measure today's firms, online markets, service quality or the full reason for the price difference.
evidence_check.location: Jones, Logan, Rosé and Cook, Competition and Consumer Discrimination, NBER Working Paper 33547, checked 2026-09-11.

nodes.title: Competition can protect the customers most able to leave
nodes.summary: Competition may change firm behavior unevenly when different customer groups have different power to switch.
nodes.question: Who does competition protect when customers do not have equal power?
nodes.limit: The opening evidence is historical and does not establish the current online or local-service result.

reading_paths.title: When the platform is both store and seller
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a platform's own product through search and data control into the service customers receive. Ask whether convenience today weakens choice tomorrow.
reading_paths.limit: The current studies use different platform settings and do not follow the same customer through product choice, data access, prices and long-run competition.

reading_paths.title: When competition protects some customers first
reading_paths.meaning: Follow customer power and firm competition into service and price, then ask when unequal treatment becomes a public demand for rules or enforcement.
reading_paths.limit: The current historical study and service evidence do not follow today's customer through treatment, switching, complaint and political response.

reading_paths.title: When a tariff keeps moving after the first price rise
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a tariff from the first import price into the existing pass-through evidence, then ask how the delayed domestic markup changes the price story a household sees.
reading_paths.limit: The current studies use different price measures and do not follow the same household through its basket, substitution, income and political judgment.

reading_paths.title: When a free app charges in time
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a no-money-price service into the time and attention it takes, then ask what the customer receives and what becomes harder to do.
reading_paths.limit: The current studies do not follow the same user through time use, work, care, sleep, well-being and exit.

reading_paths.title: When a data rule changes the customer exchange
reading_paths.meaning: Follow platform data from access and control into the customer's trust and service choice. Ask whether more openness gives customers a better answer or only a different data deal.
reading_paths.limit: The current model and privacy study concern different settings and do not follow one customer through data sharing, service quality and welfare.

reading_paths.title: When customer protection changes who can provide the ride
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a licensing rule into the drivers available, the platform choices customers see, and the ride they receive. Ask whether protection improves service or narrows access.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same city through licensing, driver entry, fares, search, wait time and safety.

reading_paths.title: When app convenience leaves money on the trip
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a ride from the app screen into the travel cost and the household money left afterward. Ask whether convenience hides a choice the customer could have made.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same rider through comparison, service quality, fare paid and later household room.

reading_paths.title: When the expected energy bill chooses the policy
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a policy tool into the bill people expect, then compare that belief with the household money and energy burden the policy may create or reduce.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same household from policy belief through actual bill, energy use and later political judgment.

reading_paths.title: When public help changes the story of the economy
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a benefit or benefit loss into felt household security, then ask how that feeling becomes a judgment about public help and government.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same family from benefit exposure through spending, sentiment, policy support and voting.

reading_paths.title: When place changes what a paycheck can buy
reading_paths.meaning: Follow local prices into the household's felt buying power, then ask how the remaining room changes purchases, savings or political judgment.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same household through local prices, actual purchases, moving choice and political response.

reading_paths.title: When the biggest local employer reaches the ballot
reading_paths.meaning: Follow local job dependence into work expectations and then into political judgment. Ask whether the employer's power changes what workers think is safe to support.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same worker from employer power through a message, belief change and vote.

reading_paths.title: When income risk at the top changes the price of money
reading_paths.meaning: Follow income risk among high earners into saving and the wider money system, then ask how a financial change becomes a public argument about fairness and policy.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not connect the same saving change to borrowing costs, household demand and political response.

reading_paths.title: When spending hides the cash constraint
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a spending number into the cash and credit room beneath it, then ask what daily need the household protects or gives up.
reading_paths.limit: The current study and food packet do not identify the same purchase, household constraint and later food outcome.

reading_paths.title: When a work benefit changes the household balance sheet
reading_paths.meaning: Follow automatic saving from the workplace into the household's account and debt position, then ask whether the job gives people more security or less room today.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same worker through take-home pay, spending, credit-card repayment and later retirement security.

reading_paths.title: When a record starts making the future
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a score change into the record a lender sees, then into housing access. The test is whether a paper signal adds a real cost before a new household failure occurs.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same borrower from score movement through lender terms, payment, housing and recovery.

reading_paths.title: When a bank fee becomes a wider credit problem
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a low-cash account through a bank fee rule and into later borrowing or payment cost. The key question is whether relief stays with the household or moves to another product.
reading_paths.limit: The current bank study and credit packet use different records and do not follow one household from the first shortage through every later cost.

reading_paths.title: When the tap becomes part of the health and housing story
reading_paths.meaning: Follow water quality from public investment into the condition of a home and then into health. Ask whether a place can look affordable while a basic service shifts risk and cost onto families.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same household from water quality to bottled-water spending, home value, care or health. The path is a connected question, not a proven chain.

reading_paths.title: When a lower bill hides an unmet need
reading_paths.meaning: Compare going without insurance, skipping treatment and relying on family help. Spending alone may miss what a household has given up.
reading_paths.limit: These studies concern different groups. They do not show that an insurance bill caused a missed treatment or more family care.

reading_paths.title: From family time to money and economic views
reading_paths.meaning: Follow three separate questions: who has time to work, what money is available, and how people judge the economy. The timing of each change matters.
reading_paths.limit: Caregiving and benefit-loss studies examine different events. We have not shown that caregiving leads to borrowing, political distrust or a changed vote.

reading_paths.title: When staying does not mean being satisfied
reading_paths.meaning: Compare continued app use with repeated requests for help. Ask whether people stay because they benefit, cannot leave, or still need an answer; then separately test any change in trust.
reading_paths.limit: Time spent is not proof of satisfaction or harm. A link from unresolved service problems to political trust remains untested.

reading_paths.title: When the same job gives people different tools
reading_paths.meaning: Follow AI access from the worker's task to the customer's answer and then to the customer's ability to continue or leave. The firm may gain speed while workers and customers face different choices.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not link worker AI access to customer exit behavior or show who gained control.

reading_paths.title: When protection becomes another household bill
reading_paths.meaning: Follow the cost of keeping a home protected into the wider payment burden, then ask how households judge the economy. The path joins two kinds of bills without treating them as one measure.
reading_paths.limit: The current packets do not track the same households across insurance payments, other payment choices and economic views.

reading_paths.title: When energy cost starts inside the home
reading_paths.meaning: Follow the building and utility bill into the wider household budget. The path asks whether energy burden changes the room left for other costs.
reading_paths.limit: The current packets do not track the same households across energy bills, housing protection and payment choices.

reading_paths.title: When a household bill becomes a balance
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a household cost from the bill to the decision to borrow, then ask what later payment or access changes.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow one household from an energy or housing bill through borrowing and repayment.

reading_paths.title: When the budget reaches the dinner table
reading_paths.meaning: Follow household cost pressure into food, then ask what health or care choice may follow.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources use different households and time windows; they do not show that a specific bill caused a specific food or health change.

reading_paths.title: When help disappears before the need does
reading_paths.meaning: Follow food need through the rules and practical work of keeping public help, then ask whether employment actually changes.
reading_paths.limit: The current studies do not follow the same household from program loss to food, debt or work outcomes.

reading_paths.title: When family care becomes paid-work time
reading_paths.meaning: Separate elder or family help from childcare, then follow the time cost into paid work and control over the household schedule.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same household across care type, cost, work hours and later income.

reading_paths.title: When a trusted service becomes a dispute
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a customer problem from the account or payment system to the effort to recover money, then ask when private frustration becomes a public demand.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow one consumer from fraud through recovery and a change in trust or political behavior.

reading_paths.title: When the trip is part of the price
reading_paths.meaning: Follow household energy and transportation cost into the time and money needed to reach work or services.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not show which households can change mode, move closer or absorb a vehicle repair.

reading_paths.title: When education debt follows the first job
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a credit claim from education into payment trouble, then ask what room remains for housing and other adult choices.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same borrower from education debt through payment, housing and work.

reading_paths.title: When household choices become a judgment about the country
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a price or benefit change into the household action, then keep personal finances, national economic views and trust as separate steps.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not show that a specific price or benefit change caused a change in trust, voting or policy demand.

reading_paths.title: When family care becomes a work decision
reading_paths.meaning: Follow unpaid eldercare into paid work, earnings and the choices made around the household schedule.
reading_paths.limit: The current time-use data show overlap, not whether care changed employment or employment changed who provided care.

reading_paths.title: When a business idea leaves home
reading_paths.meaning: Follow housing and local cost conditions into where founders live, then ask whether business activity becomes lasting local jobs and services.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not show that owner movement changed a place's services, jobs, prices or belonging.

reading_paths.title: When the energy bill begins with the home
reading_paths.meaning: Follow the home and its energy burden into the household's room for other payments, then ask whether credit absorbs the gap.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same household from energy burden through arrears, borrowing or a later housing choice.

reading_paths.title: When service speed meets the need for an appeal
reading_paths.meaning: Follow the worker's AI tool into the customer's first answer, then ask who can fix a disputed loss or decision.
reading_paths.limit: The current studies do not connect worker AI use to customer remedy, appeal or fraud recovery in one setting.

reading_paths.title: When workplace fit becomes a work gate
reading_paths.meaning: Follow familiar speech from access to people-facing work into the worker's role and the service customers receive.
reading_paths.limit: The current evidence does not connect speech, a manager's decision, worker advancement and customer results in one record.

reading_paths.title: When career movement slows around a long payment
reading_paths.meaning: Follow measured career movement into the room left for education debt and then housing choices.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same worker from career level through debt payment and housing.

reading_paths.title: When an ownership promise meets the paycheck
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a worker's financial claim into daily work and then ask whether it becomes pay, savings or only a reason to stay.
reading_paths.limit: The current evidence does not show actual payouts, household wealth or worker control after the retention change.

reading_paths.title: When one office day changes the remote week
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a planned office meeting into later coworker contact and then count the travel time and cost it requires.
reading_paths.limit: The current trial does not show which workers benefit after travel cost, care duty, disability, distance and job type are included.

reading_paths.title: When getting help becomes a social choice
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a person's choice to use or avoid a habit-change aid into attention and then ask how products and institutions make help feel normal or exposing.
reading_paths.limit: The current evidence supports social judgment in controlled tasks but does not follow the same US consumers through tool use and later behavior.

reading_paths.title: When a forgotten subscription becomes a household cost
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a recurring charge that survives after its value fades into the household budget, then ask whether repeated private costs become a public trust question.
reading_paths.limit: The NBER estimate is model-based and does not follow the same US customer from an unwanted renewal to a changed budget or political view.

reading_paths.title: When the shape of aid changes the household week
reading_paths.meaning: Follow the form and timing of public help into food spending, then ask whether short-run spending becomes real security or only a different kind of constraint.
reading_paths.limit: The new study measures short-run food-store spending and does not follow the same families through broader needs, lasting security or political response.

reading_paths.title: When the price people see becomes the economy they judge
reading_paths.meaning: Follow repeated prices and wage comparisons into the household's sense of room, then ask when that private loss becomes a public judgment.
reading_paths.limit: The sources measure survey beliefs and retail price patterns separately; they do not follow the same household into a political response.

reading_paths.title: When trade policy becomes a delayed shelf price
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a tariff from policy to shelf price, then into the repeated price and wage comparisons that shape a household's sense of room.
reading_paths.limit: The current studies use product prices and separate surveys; they do not follow one household from a tariff change to a purchase, budget change or political judgment.

reading_paths.title: When equal income buys a different life
reading_paths.meaning: Follow several jobs into spending, travel and saving, then ask whether flexibility is replacing stability rather than adding to it.
reading_paths.limit: The current evidence does not follow the same worker from job structure through net income, household choices and later security.

reading_paths.title: When staying with a bank becomes a household choice
reading_paths.meaning: Follow the effort of moving a deposit into the interest and household room left behind, then ask whether repeated quiet costs shape views of financial institutions.
reading_paths.limit: The current evidence models bank value and stability but does not follow the same US depositor from a missed rate to a changed budget or political view.

reading_paths.title: When privacy protection increases the data exchange
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a privacy rule into a person's willingness to use a service and share data, then ask whether the new trust changes public expectations of firms and government.
reading_paths.limit: The current study measures sharing on one app and does not show later data use, service outcomes or political response.

reading_paths.title: When local buying power reaches the ballot
reading_paths.meaning: Follow local prices and wages into the household's sense of room, then ask whether lost buying power becomes a vote against the party in power.
reading_paths.limit: The current study uses county outcomes and separate price beliefs; it does not show the same household's costs, blame, trust or vote.

reading_paths.title: When business ownership moves away from home
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a founder's move into local ownership and then ask how housing, services and place control change for the people who remain.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources measure birthplace ties, home equity and business entry separately; they do not follow residents through a local change.

reading_paths.title: When a rate decision becomes a household belief
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a central-bank decision into what households expect about prices and borrowing, then into spending, saving and financial room.
reading_paths.limit: The current studies use randomized information and reported expectations; they do not follow the same household's policy exposure, financial records and trust.

reading_paths.title: When age hides different kinds of need
reading_paths.meaning: Follow differences in health, independence and buying power into care and household money, then ask whether firms serve or sort older customers fairly.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources describe segments, spending and health risk separately; they do not follow the same older customer through a product or care decision.

reading_paths.title: When emotional support becomes an attention system
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a private AI reply into time spent and the ability to leave, then ask whether the service offers safe care or mainly continued engagement.
reading_paths.limit: The current studies mix prevention and companion apps and do not follow the same user through long-term well-being, crisis care or exit.

reading_paths.title: When a car repair becomes a household timing shock
reading_paths.meaning: Follow an unexpected repair into the cash buffer, then ask what happens to the route to work, care and food when the vehicle is stopped.
reading_paths.limit: The opening sources do not follow the same household from a repair to a missed trip, lost work or later debt.

reading_paths.title: When family help catches the fall
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a shock from one household into money or unpaid care from another, then ask who has less room afterward.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources show changes in family support but do not follow both sides through work, debt and later security.

reading_paths.title: When the family and the business share one cash pool
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a business or family shock into the owner's protection choice, then ask what happens to business investment and household room.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same owner through the choice and later jobs, services or family wealth.

reading_paths.title: When a raise changes the help a family can keep
reading_paths.meaning: Follow an earnings change into the public help that falls away, then ask whether the household has more room and more stable work afterward.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same family through total resources, care costs and work after the change.

reading_paths.title: When the due date is part of the energy burden
reading_paths.meaning: Follow the gap between income and the utility due date into arrears or shutoff, then ask what payment, credit or health cost follows.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not establish the full later chain for every household.

reading_paths.title: When health coverage keeps a job in place
reading_paths.meaning: Follow employer coverage into the cost of changing jobs, then ask whether the worker gains or gives up pay, fit and family care access.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not compare the full job and coverage choice for the same worker.

reading_paths.title: When debt relief fixes the record but not the illness
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a medical bill into the credit record, then ask whether relief changes the household's later room even when the health need remains.
reading_paths.limit: The current experiment does not connect the credit result to every later housing, work or care choice.

reading_paths.title: When cash changes the shape of a household
reading_paths.meaning: Follow regular cash into rent or mortgage arrears and who lives together, then ask whether the added room lasts after the payment ends.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not show that a smaller or changed household is safer or better for every family.

reading_paths.title: When a benefit loss changes the public mood
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a household benefit from cash loss into consumer sentiment, then ask whether trust, blame or voting changes later.
reading_paths.limit: The current study measures sentiment and does not establish the later political step.

reading_paths.title: When the same yearly income buys less certainty
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a change in pay risk into spending and credit, then ask whether the household can still plan, borrow and keep its choices open.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not follow the same worker through pay risk, cash reserves and later household outcomes.

reading_paths.title: When a temporary payment becomes a monthly bill
reading_paths.meaning: Follow a one-time payment into a vehicle or other durable purchase, then ask whether financing protects access or narrows later room.
reading_paths.limit: The current sources do not show the same household's need, loan terms and later repayment outcome.
